headline: High-risk shared-project and runtime overlap: default write paths and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write project files, and agent_a shares state via the project directory while agent_b shares state via mounted volume. That creates a default content bridge where attacker-controlled files from either side can be treated as instructions. No provenance tracking is documented, so injection is plausible without extra setup.
conditions: IF agent_a writes instructions into the shared project directory and agent_b later parses them as task text
IF agent_b writes attacker-controlled content into the mounted volume and agent_a reads it as trusted file content
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different project directories or volumes
Add a manual review step before either agent consumes files written by the other
Prefix shared files with provenance labels and ignore unlabeled instructions
Disable automatic task ingestion from shared files
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware filtering between the two agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a touches generated source code in a shared project directory, and agent_b reads files in a runtime sandbox with mounted-volume sharing. Because both have broad network egress, any sensitive code or secrets placed in shared files can flow into model calls or outbound requests. The profiles do not show a hard isolation boundary between their file surfaces.
conditions: IF sensitive source code or secrets are stored in the shared project directory or mounted volume
IF either agent includes shared file contents in prompts or outbound API calls
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace
Use separate per-agent workspaces with no mounted-volume overlap
Redact sensitive files before either agent reads them
Restrict outbound network access during file review tasks
requires-engineering: enforce file-level access controls between the two runtimes

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, execute shells, spawn subprocesses, and use overlapping project state. Agent_b also modifies git state, while agent_a writes files then offers to run code. In a shared directory, concurrent edits and git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt the workspace, and the profiles do not document locking.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory or mounted volume at the same time
IF agent_b commits or rewrites git state while agent_a is also writing files
mitigations: Run the agents on separate branches or separate directories
Serialize write access with a simple operator-managed lock
Disable git mutations for one agent during shared tasks
Take a snapshot before concurrent edits
requires-engineering: add workspace locking and conflict detection

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_a writes files and offers to run generated code, while agent_b has a broader agent loop with browser, shell, and MCP access. If agent_b treats agent_a's outputs as authoritative, mistakes or malicious content can cascade into actions, commits, or external requests. The interaction is undocumented, so uncertainty should be treated conservatively.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a's generated files or claims without verification
IF agent_b uses those outputs to browse, edit, commit, or call external APIs
mitigations: Require explicit human review before agent_b acts on agent_a output
Add a verification checklist for generated facts and code
Limit agent_b to read-only inspection when ingesting agent_a artifacts
Log and diff all downstream actions triggered by agent_a outputs
requires-engineering: add structured provenance and validation gates

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source coding agents with docs-only evidence and no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch documented. The main compliance concern is shared handling of generated source code and model-provider secrets, but the profiles do not show a specific regulated-data pathway. The other agent is cited because the risk is about the pair's shared workspace and outbound calls.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared workspace or runtime files
IF either agent's configured model provider or logging policy retains that data beyond the operator's intended scope
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Review provider retention settings before running either agent
Use separate environments for regulated and non-regulated work
Delete temporary files after each task
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls for both agents
